did_you_know.text: The chapter opens with the word “oracle,” referring to a prophecy or weighty proclamation, and concerns Babylon, as foretold by Isaiah son of Amoz.
The LORD is portrayed as a commander who summons his “warriors” and appoints them to carry out his judgment, so that the human army is depicted as an instrument in his hand.
The prophecy describes a gathering of many peoples and kingdoms—not just a single army—for the campaign against Babylon.
The forces come “from a distant land” and from the ends of the heavens, emphasizing the scale of the threat and the distance from which they come.
The expression “the day of the LORD” describes an imminent day of plunder, destruction, and wrath—not a day of celebration or rest.
The description of the sun, moon, and stars being darkened uses cosmic imagery to express the intensity of the crisis and judgment.
The stated purpose of the judgment is to punish the wickedness of the world and the wicked, and to humble the pride of the arrogant and tyrants.
The prophecy compares the scattering of Babylon’s inhabitants to a fleeing gazelle and sheep without a shepherd; each person turns to their own people or flees to their own land.
The Medes are mentioned as a force rising against Babylon and are described as warriors who place no value on silver and cannot be bribed.

Babylon, described as the “jewel of kingdoms” and the pride of the Chaldeans, is compared to the destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah; at the end of the chapter, it is portrayed as a desolate place inhabited by animals instead of people.
